newsitem.title: USA: PG&E to sell four more California power plants.
newsitem.headline: PG&E to sell four more California power plants.

text.p: PG&E Corp., the parent of San Francisco-based Pacific Gas & Electric Co., said Tuesday it plans to sell four more of its California power plants as part of the state's plan to deregulate its electricity industry.

The move brings to eight the number of power plants PG&E is selling to meet the California Public Utilities Commission's orders that PG&E divest 50 percent of its fossil-fuelled power generation assets.
"Pacific Gas & Electric Co.'s sale of these four additional plants will further the development of a competitive generation industry in California," PG&E President Gordon Smith said in a statement.
"This is another example of PG&E's transition from a vertically integrated monopoly to a distribution company," he added.
A total of 446 jobs will be affected.
Smith said plans for the sale would be sent to the California Public Utilities Commission later this year and that he hopes to have buyers lined up for the units by the end of 1998.
"Together, the (eight) plants represent 98 percent of PG&E's fossil-fuelled generating capacity, as well as the company's only geothermal facility," the statement said.

The latest batch of power plants being offered have an overall generating capacity of 4,289 megawatts. They include the Pittsburg Power Plant (2,022 MW), the Contra Costa Power Plant in Antioch (680 MW), and the Potrero Power Plant in San Francisco (363 MW).
Also being offered is PG&E's geothermal power plant at The Geysers (1,224 MW) in Sonoma and Lake Counties north of San Francisco.
In October 1996, PG&E offered to sell its power plants at Hunters Point (426 MW) in San Francisco, Morro Bay (1,002 MW), Moss Landing (1,478 MW) and Oakland Power Plant (153 MW). Each is gas-fired.
PG&E said it is still awaiting CPUC approval to move ahead with the sale of the first four plants.

The decision to divest the plants was sparked by a CPUC directive that California's utilities voluntarily sell off at least half of the fossil-fuelled power plants in their respective service territories. This is a main part of the state's strategy to build up a competitive power generation industry separate from distribution and transmission, which will remain in the hands of traditional utilities.
PG&E, one of the nation's largest investor-owned electric and gas utilities, serves nearly 13 million people in northern and central California.
PG&E's stock edged up 12.5 cents to $23.75 on the New York Stock Exchange at mid-afternoon.
